dimension_1_problem_framing.text: The paper targets the core quantitative finance task of determining fair prices for financial derivatives, focusing on the Black–Scholes equation as the standard PDE model for European-style options and casting it as a Schrödinger-type equation with an arbitrary non-Hermitian Hamiltonian amenable to quantum simulation. The authors frame non-unitary (non-Hermitian) time evolution as the key barrier to directly simulating such PDEs on quantum computers and seek a formulation that can handle general non-Hermitian dynamics rather than only special anti-Hermitian cases.

dimension_2_quantum_method.text: The proposed method is QNUTE, a generalisation of simulated quantum imaginary-time evolution (QITE) to simulate Schrödinger dynamics with arbitrary non-Hermitian Hamiltonians, implemented via a first-order Trotter product of non-unitary time-evolution operators whose normalised actions are approximated by local unitaries determined from measurement-constructed linear systems. The approach encodes discretised Black–Scholes option prices as amplitudes of an n-qubit state using a finite-difference Hamiltonian with boundary conditions embedded directly into the operator, and it includes both an exact version with domain size equal to the full qubit register and an inexact variant that constrains the local unitary domain size D < n to trade accuracy for reduced measurement and circuit overhead. Resource scaling is described in terms of the number of measurements and circuit depth per Trotter step, and the authors note that state expressivity and accuracy depend critically on the choice of operator basis and the size of the local domain used in the unitary approximation.

dimension_3_key_results.text: Using statevector simulations, the authors report that QNUTE can match analytical solutions of the Black–Scholes equation across multiple option types when using full-domain unitaries, including a boundary-rescaling protocol derived from solving a linear ODE for the option price near the asset-price boundaries. They find that convergence and accuracy depend on placing domain boundaries so that linear boundary conditions hold for the payoff and having sufficient discretisation points near strike prices; they also empirically observe that the discretised Black–Scholes Hamiltonian exhibits high qubit-to-qubit correlation, and that inexact QNUTE with fixed small domain size D fails to capture these correlations as the number of qubits increases, leading to degraded fidelity. Quantitative results summarised as average fidelities for different (n, D) configurations show that fidelity remains near 1.0 when D scales with n (e.g., D = n) but can drop substantially for larger systems when D is kept small.

dimension_4_classical_comparison.text: The paper compares QNUTE-generated option prices against analytical Black–Scholes solutions as a correctness benchmark but does not present any runtime or resource comparison to classical numerical PDE solvers. The authors emphasise that their approach directly solves the original Black–Scholes equation without post-selection, distinguishing it conceptually from earlier quantum schemes, yet no claims of classical speedup or advantage are empirically demonstrated.

dimension_5_stated_limitations.text: The authors highlight that simulating non-Hermitian (non-unitary) dynamics is not directly feasible on quantum hardware, motivating their approximation framework and implying practical complexity. They acknowledge limitations of existing variational QITE methods, including dependence on ansatz expressivity and barren plateaus, and note that simulated QITE (and hence QNUTE) can require an exponential number of measurements in the locality parameter k, with QNUTE’s measurement cost scaling exponentially with domain size D due to I = O(2^D) basis elements. Accuracy in QNUTE depends on the support of the local unitary (domain size), leading to inexact implementations when D is fixed below the full system size; experiments show that for increasing qubit counts and fixed D, inexact QNUTE fails to capture long-range correlations inherent in the discretised Black–Scholes Hamiltonian, degrading fidelity. The Pauli decomposition of the Black–Scholes operator itself incurs an exponential growth in the number of distinct Pauli strings with qubit number, signalling a scalability bottleneck that the authors state requires alternative decompositions. On the modelling side, they assume constant volatility and interest rates and caution that stochastic or time-dependent parameters may necessitate smaller time steps and changes to the boundary ODE and rescaling protocol. They further note that convergence quality is sensitive to the placement of asset-price boundaries (which must ensure the validity of linear boundary conditions) and to having enough grid points near strike prices, with poor resolution near strikes notably degrading accuracy in low-qubit simulations. Finally, they indicate that while their method avoids post-selection used in prior work, this does not remove the underlying complexity challenges around measurement cost and Hamiltonian representation.

dimension_6_future_work.text: For scalability, the authors argue that an alternative, more compact Hamiltonian decomposition is required for Black–Scholes and conjecture that adopting a recently proposed linear-overhead measurement scheme could yield exponentially fewer Hamiltonian terms within their framework. They also plan to incorporate recent improvements to simulated QITE into QNUTE and hint that extending their rescaling protocol and time-discretisation strategies will be necessary to handle more realistic, time-dependent or stochastic financial parameters.

dimension_7_novelty_claim.text: The key novelty claim is the generalisation of simulated QITE to quantum non-unitary time evolution (QNUTE), which removes the restriction to anti-Hermitian Hamiltonians and is intended to handle arbitrary non-Hermitian PDEs formulated as Schrödinger equations, with the Black–Scholes equation provided as a primary example. The authors assert that, unlike prior quantum Black–Scholes approaches that approximate non-unitary dynamics with unitary operators or rely on post-selection, their method directly solves the original non-Hermitian Black–Scholes PDE without post-selection while maintaining a general non-unitary simulation framework.

dimension_8_methodological_notes.text: Methodologically, the work is purely simulation-based on ideal statevector hardware and does not report experiments on noisy quantum devices, though the broader QITE/varQITE context is noted as suitable for NISQ hardware. The authors provide explicit construction details: amplitude encoding of discretised option prices, central and one-sided finite-difference schemes for the Black–Scholes Hamiltonian, incorporation of linear boundary conditions via modified matrix rows, and a boundary-rescaling protocol derived from solving an ODE, all of which support conceptual reproducibility even though code is not provided. They discuss resource scaling analytically (measurements and circuit depth per Trotter step, and exponential dependence on domain size and Pauli term count), and systematically explore fidelity behaviour under different domain sizes D and qubit counts, but do not benchmark against classical solvers or report wall-clock performance, so the study focuses on correctness and scaling characteristics rather than end-to-end practical performance.

dimension_9_miscellaneous.text: The authors situate their work within the broader narrative that quantum computing has the potential to transform financial technology and reiterate that the Black–Scholes model is the standard reference for European option pricing, using this to motivate their choice of test problem and the broader relevance of non-Hermitian PDE simulation to quantum finance.
